Participants (Methods)

uncertain_note: c2/flags: R2 is undecided by the protocol on this text and is coded false. The work's only vendor mention is the in-text parenthetical identifying the administered tool (R1). It carries no citation, and the reference list contains no vendor entry. But the note under Table 1 explains the four type letters using the aspect names Mind / nature / energy / tactics: "Note: The four letters represent the traits of personality, which describe Mind (Introversive or Extroversive), nature (iNtuition or Sensing), energy (Thinking or Feeling), and tactics (Perception or Judging)." (Table 1 note, 2. Methods, 2.1 Participants). Those aspect labels are the vendor's own naming of the dimensions and appear in no published MBTI form, so on the wide reading §6 fixes for the C flags ("Like §5, this step covers the vendor's test, its site, and its proprietary content") the work would be sourcing its account of the MBTI's dichotomies to the vendor's material, which is R2. title: Use of Personality Frameworks in Health Science Education.
quote_e: Based on this systematic review, there is little published evidence that instructors and preceptors are using personality frameworks as a tool for self-awareness in health sciences education. — Discussion
free_text: c2/gate: E4 by §2 ("reviews"): the work is a PRISMA-guided literature review whose data are extracted from 71 included articles, not from respondents — "After screening titles, abstracts, and/or the full text of the 415 articles identified in an initial search, 71 articles involving personality frameworks were included in the study." — Abstract. Twelve of the reviewed studies used the MBTI ("The next most used test was the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI), used in 12 studies (17%)." — RESULTS), but those administrations belong to the cited studies, not to this work (§5 amendment of 2026-08-19), so they carry no R1. The vendor URL appears in the reference list (reference 54), but §4.1 / c-vendor-cited-only applies only to E1 works, so it does not reach the instrument step. || c2/flags: The vendor appears exactly three times in the retrieved text and nowhere else: the in-text list of future-direction frameworks in Discussion, the reference-list entry 54, and the URL inside that entry. The work administered nothing (a literature review), analyses 71 other articles' use of frameworks, and none of its claims are sourced to the vendor, so R1-R5 fail; the vendor is also not what the work analyses or measures attitudes toward (its subject is the health-science-education literature on personality frameworks generally, and 16 Personalities is named only as a framework nobody in that literature had yet used), so R7 fails and the mention is R6. No R7 was set even though the sentence is about the vendor as a possible future instrument, because the work neither analyses it nor measures attitudes toward it. The MBTI passages in the Introduction ('The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) details 16 different personality types based on an individual's preferences for perception and judgement. 8') are sourced to The Myers & Briggs Foundation (references 6 and 8), not to the vendor, and no vendor proprietary content appears anywhere: no Assertive/Turbulent axis, no Analyst/Diplomat/Sentinel/Explorer groupings, no branded type names. The only type abbreviation used, 'ENTJ', is a published-MBTI type code. Hence C0 under both the wide and the narrow reading. states_distinction was left false as a borderline call: the work does place '16 Personalities' in a list of frameworks separate from the MBTI it had described earlier, but it never states anywhere that the vendor's test and the MBTI are not the same instrument, and no sentence in the text can be quoted as such a statement — the separation is an implication of the layout, not an assertion. 'A similar test to the MBTI is the cognitive-experiential self-theory (CEST)' calls CEST similar to the MBTI but does not call it the MBTI, so third_party_conflation is false. No bundled citation was flagged on more than one role. This work is not one of the three calibration records in §7.

title: Do we behave differently on Twitter and Facebook: Multi-view social network user personality profiling for content recommendation.
quote_e: "Ground truth collection . To obtain personality ground truth from Twitter , we have downloaded all tweets that contain self-reported personality-related keywords/phrases such as “I'm an ENTP ” or “I am an ENTP ” and extracted the personality trait from those phrases. This trait represents the ground truth for each user (see Figure 1A for an example). To harvest Facebook ground truth, we have monitored Facebook comments under personality test results released on the 16personalities portal (see Figure 1B for an example). Likewise, to obtain personality-related ground truth from the PersonalityCafe forum, we downloaded the users' publicly available self-reported personality traits from their profile pages (see Figure 1C for an example)." — Section 3.2.1 Data acquisition (Ground truth collection)
uncertain_note: c2/gate: The conflation coding is the undecided part. §6 requires a located conflation *statement*, and this work contains no single sentence that names the 16personalities test and the MBTI as one instrument, gives the vendor's test the MBTI's lineage, or calls it official/validated. The vendor is named exactly once, as a place where results were released. So on a sentence-level reading the code is C0, which is what I recorded. But the work does the conflation structurally: §3.1 states "To represent human personality, in this work we use the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) (Myers, 1998 ), widely adopted by the research community (Buraya et al., 2017 , 2018 ).", and the Facebook arm of its ground truth is harvested from "personality test results released on the 16personalities portal", after which those labels are pooled with the Twitter and PersonalityCafe labels into one MBTI 16-type space (Table 2) and reported as MBTI types. A coder reading §6 substantively rather than sentence-by-sentence could code C1 on that basis. §6 does not say whether a conflation enacted across two sections of Methods, with no single sentence carrying it, counts; I did not invent a rule, so I coded C0 and am flagging it for adjudication. || c2/flags: Undecided item: whether C1 can be established by a chain when the work never identifies the two instruments in any single statement. The work contains exactly one vendor mention, and it is the sole source of the Facebook arm's ground-truth type labels, which the work then reports and evaluates as MBTI types. The chain a reader could build is: Section 3.1 MBTI personality categorization: "To represent human personality, in this work we use the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) (Myers, 1998 ), widely adopted by the research community (Buraya et al., 2017 , 2018 )." || Section 3.2 PERS multi-source multi-view personality dataset: "Thus, we collected the primary dataset for this work from social networks for users whose personality types are somehow known; in this section, we outline data acquisition and feature extraction (preprocessing) for this dataset." || Section 3.2.1 Data acquisition, 'Ground truth collection': "To harvest Facebook ground truth, we have monitored Facebook comments under personality test results released on the 16personalities portal (see Figure 1B for an example)." || Section 5.3 heading and opening sentence: "5.3. Evaluation across MBTI categories To evaluate the performance of the PERS framework in a real-world scenario, we have evaluated the limits of PERS performance across Twitter, Facebook , and PersonalityCafe datasets." On that chain the work treats the vendor's test output as MBTI type data, which is arguably "treats the vendor's test and the MBTI as one instrument" (Section 6, opening). I coded C0 rather than C1 because Section 6's chain rule is written as propagation from an identification that the work has already made in words -- "A work that names the two as one instrument in Methods and gives the MBTI a Jungian lineage in the Introduction has made the lineage claim about the vendor's test, by its own identification" -- and this work makes no such naming act anywhere: the vendor is named once, in a data-provenance sentence, and the MBTI is never equated with it in any sentence. Reading the chain rule as able to manufacture an identity claim rather than propagate one would be inventing a rule, and Section 12 records that where the protocol did not decide, the reading that weakens the headline was taken; C1 here would add to M2's numerator. A second consideration: Section 5's R5 exists for exactly this shape ("where labels or profiles were scraped from or matched to"), so treating every vendor-sourced label set as an automatic C1 would collapse the two steps. The item is flagged for adjudication because the counter-reading is substantive, not because the quotes are unclear. Note also that if C1 were set, it would be set under both the wide and the narrow reading, since the supporting statement names the vendor's site by name and the work uses none of the vendor's proprietary content (no -A/-T axis, no Analyst/Diplomat groupings, no branded type names -- only the four classic dichotomies and the sixteen four-letter codes).
free_text: c1/gate: The work's type ground truth is assembled from three distinct scraped sources, none administered by the authors: (1) Twitter self-report keyword phrases such as "I'm an ENTP" or "I am an ENTP"; (2) Facebook comments under personality test results posted on the 16personalities portal; (3) PersonalityCafe users' self-reported personality traits from their own profile pages (Section 3.2.1, Data acquisition). Only the Facebook source names the vendor (16personalities); it is cited only as the origin of scraped labels (R5), not as something the authors or the Facebook users administered as part of this study. Section 3.1 ("MBTI personality categorization") cites Myers (1998), the published MBTI Manual, for the theoretical framework of four binary dimensions (EI, SN, TF, JP) that is applied uniformly to all three sources' labels; this citation is to the actual manual, not the vendor, so it does not carry an R flag. No sentence anywhere in the retrieved text names the 16personalities portal and the MBTI/Myers-Briggs instrument as the same thing, gives the vendor's test a disclaimed Jung/Myers-Briggs lineage, or calls it official/standard/validated/professional, hence C0 rather than C1/C2/C3, though the paper's uniform framing of all labels under an "MBTI" umbrella (including the 16personalities-sourced Facebook labels) is worth flagging for the adjudicator as the closest thing to an implicit conflation in this text. || c1/flags: The only vendor mention in the whole retrieved text (including the reference list and footnotes) is the single sentence quoted for R5. That sentence never uses the word MBTI. Section 3.1 separately states 'To represent human personality, in this work we use the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) (Myers, 1998)' and Section 3.2.1 treats the 16personalities-portal-derived Facebook comments as one of three interchangeable 'ground truth' sources feeding that same MBTI-labeled dataset (alongside self-reported Twitter hashtags/phrases and PersonalityCafe profile pages). No single sentence, and no chain of sentences with an identifying anchor comparable to the Koshiro or Tshimula calibration records, names the 16personalities test and the MBTI as one instrument, gives the vendor's test the MBTI's provenance, or claims the vendor's test has the MBTI's standing. On that basis C0/C1/C2/C3 were coded as no conflation, but the pattern (vendor-scraped labels folded into an undifferentiated 'MBTI' dataset without ever naming the source instrument in the same breath) is noted here for the record. || c2/gate: E2 rather than E1: the authors administered nothing. All three label sources are harvested — Twitter self-reports mined from tweet text ("I'm an ENTP"), Facebook comments posted under 16personalities results, and self-reported traits on PersonalityCafe profile pages. The vendor's test therefore appears only as the origin of one of three scraped label streams, which is why R5 is the only role flag set. The MBTI constructs themselves are sourced to Myers 1998, MBTI Manual, not to the vendor, so R2 is not set for the vendor. The vendor is mentioned exactly once in the whole text ("the 16personalities portal"); there is no vendor URL in the reference list. No instrument code applies (§2: only E1 works receive one). A second, non-administered arm exists in the sense that the paper's own PERS model *infers* MBTI dimensions for users from text and images, but that is a classifier output, not an instrument administered to anyone, so it is not E3. || c2/flags: Whole-text sweep for vendor word forms (16personalities, 16 Personalities, NERIS, Type Explorer, personalities.com) returns exactly one hit, the Section 3.2.1 sentence quoted for R5. The vendor has no reference-list entry; the mention is in-text only, so Section 5's reference-list-only rule does not apply and no bundled citation is involved. Scope of the vendor's role: it supplies ground truth for the Facebook arm only. The Twitter arm's labels come from self-reported tweets ("we have downloaded all tweets that contain self-reported personality-related keywords/phrases such as “I'm an ENTP ” or “I am an ENTP ”") and the PersonalityCafe arm's from forum profile pages, neither of which involves the vendor. R1 was considered and rejected: this work administered nothing to anybody: it harvested existing self-reported labels, so the vendor's site is a data source and not an administered instrument. R6 was considered and rejected because a substantive claim of the work -- one third of its ground-truth data -- rests on the vendor mention. R7 was considered and rejected: the vendor is not the object of study; the objects of study are the PERS framework and cross-platform behavioural differences. The work is a single Frontiers article with no neighbouring works bundled in the retrieved file, so Section 3.6's one-file-several-works rule does not bite. C3 was considered on "widely adopted by the research community": rejected on two independent grounds -- it is said of the MBTI, not of the vendor's test, and Section 6 puts uptake claims outside C3. states_distinction is false: the work nowhere notes that the vendor's test and the MBTI are different instruments; its one hedge, "users whose personality types are somehow known", declines to name any instrument rather than drawing the distinction. This work is not one of the three calibration records in Section 7.

(1) Instrument sub-label: Methods 2.1 names what was administered as 'the Keirsey Temperament Classifier, a shortened version of the Myers–Briggs Temperament Indicator (MBTI)', with a '70 statements with two response options' scale given in Slovenian. This is level-1 Methods evidence, and it is neither (a) [not 16Personalities/NERIS — never mentioned as administered] nor (b) [not Form M/G/Q/Step I/II, no purchase/licence/certified-administration statement] under §3.2–3.3, so it falls to (c) by elimination. But the §3.4 sub-labels are built around an *unidentified* instrument (c-unnamed, c-online, c-vendor-cited-only) or one *the authors wrote* (c-authormade), and this work names a real, existing, distinct instrument (the Keirsey Temperament Sorter) rather than leaving it unnamed or inventing it. I coded c-translated because the questionnaire was administered in Slovenian with no license or original source stated for that translation, which is the closest fit, but a named third-party non-MBTI, non-vendor instrument self-described as 'a shortened version of the MBTI' is not a scenario any sub-label describes cleanly. (2) Conflation: Table 2 (in the Introduction, before Methods) is captioned 'Groups according to MBTI (adopted from Kiersley [10])' and its second column is headed 'Modern Denomination (Summarized by 16 Personalities)', mapping Keirsey's four temperament groups to 16Personalities' own group names (Explorer, Sentinel, Diplomat, Analyst). A stricter reading, given the table's own caption frames both columns as 'Groups according to MBTI', could support C2; I left it C0 and flag the disagreement for adjudication. || c2/gate: Two points are not cleanly decided by the protocol. (1) Instrument code and sub-label. Methods state that respondents completed the Keirsey Temperament Classifier, described by the authors as "a shortened version of the Myers–Briggs Temperament Indicator (MBTI)". That is a named third instrument: no §3.2 trigger for (a) appears anywhere (the sole 16 Personalities word form is the Table 2 column header, not a statement of what was administered; there is no NERIS/Type Explorer mention and no vendor URL in the reference list), and no §3.3 trigger for (b) appears (no Form M/G/Q, no Step I/II, no purchase, licence or certified administration; the Myers/McCaulley manual is cited as background only, which §3.3 says is not by itself (b)). So (c) is reached by elimination on evidence level 1. But §3.4 defines (c) as "a work that administered something it does not identify", and this work does identify what it administered — it is simply not one of the two instruments the scheme names. The scheme has no code for that shape, so the (c) label over-states the gap. The sub-label is undecided for the same reason: none of the five fits exactly. I chose c-translated on §4.3, because the administered MBTI-type questionnaire was given in Slovenian with no licence and no source stated in Methods. The alternative is c-unnamed, whose test ("no form, publisher, version or URL") is also satisfied verbatim for the administered questionnaire. c1/gate: The paper analyzes two fictional Marvel movie characters (Captain America/Steve Rogers, Iron Man/Tony Stark), not real survey respondents. Alongside MBTI/NERIS Type Explorer, the authors apply several unrelated, non-MBTI typology frameworks to the same two characters and to the product/service brands appearing alongside them: Jennifer Aaker's Brand Personality dimensions, Mark & Pearson's 12 brand archetypes, Rogers' innovation-adoption curve, Jungian type theory, and the DISC model (Sections 4.1-4.4, 4.6). None of these carry a 16Personalities/vendor citation and so are out of scope for this audit's R/C flags. MBTI's own origin is described in Section 4.5 via Katharine Briggs and Isabel Briggs Myers, without a vendor-domain citation attached to that specific sentence, so it does not independently trigger an R flag; the R2/R5 flags recorded here rest specifically on the NERIS Type Explorer citations to NERIS Analytics Limited (2020, 'Our Framework') and to Monica (2019a, 2019b — the vendor's own 'Avengers Personality Series' character-typing articles, both hosted at 16personalities.com). || c1/flags: This work is a conference-proceedings book chapter (peer-reviewed) applying multiple typology frameworks (Aaker's brand-personality dimensions, Rogers' diffusion-of-innovation curve, Jungian types, DISC, Mark & Pearson archetypes, MBTI/NERIS Type Explorer) to two FICTIONAL Marvel characters (Captain America, Iron Man), not to human or agent respondents; nothing is administered in this work, so no R1. Aaker/Mark&Pearson/DISC/Rogers citations are unrelated frameworks and are not evidence for the MBTI/16Personalities R or C flags. R2 and R5 rest on two distinct vendor citations, not a single bundled one: R2 on 'NERIS Analytics Limited, 2020' (the vendor's own 'Our Framework'/'Our Theory' page, cited as the source of the five-dichotomy construct system the authors use to analyze both characters), and R5 on 'Monica, 2019a' and 'Monica, 2019b' (the vendor's own 16personalities.com 'Avengers Personality Series' articles specifically profiling Captain America as 'Defender' and Iron Man as 'Commander', which this work's own character-profile sections reproduce and build on). C2's provenance claim is explicit and unambiguous: the text states NERIS Type Explorer was 'named' by 'a módszer megalkotói' (the creators of the [MBTI] method), i.e. Katharine Cook Briggs and Isabel Briggs Myers per the immediately preceding sentence — a lineage the vendor (NERIS Analytics Limited) itself disclaims. || c2/gate: No instrument was administered to anyone: there is no human respondent arm and no language-model or other artificial-agent arm. The entities given types are two fictional film characters (Steve Rogers / Captain America, Tony Stark / Iron Man) and the product and service brands placed around them. Four further typologies are applied to the same subjects alongside the NERIS Type Explorer — Rogers' innovation adoption curve, Jung's types, DISC, the Mark and Pearson archetypes and Jennifer Aaker's five brand personality dimensions — none of them a 16Personalities or MBTI form, and none administered either. The MBTI is discussed as a model in 4.5 but no MBTI form, publisher or licence is named anywhere. §3.6 scope note: the retrieved file is the whole Sopron 2024 conference volume's front matter (cover data, organising and scientific committees, and a table of contents listing some sixty other papers) followed by this one chapter, DOI 10.35511/978-963-334-499-6-Papp-Vary-Ronky, pp. 591-608, from the Absztrakt through its own Irodalomjegyzék. Only that chapter was used as evidence; every MBTI, 16Personalities and NERIS occurrence in the file falls inside it, and the other titles appear only as table-of-contents lines. || c2/flags: Scope (Sec. 3.6): the retrieved file is the whole conference proceedings volume — cover data, organising committees, and the full table of contents of some sixty papers — plus one chapter. Only the target work was coded: PAPP-VARY Arpad Ferenc and RONKY Aron, "Márkázott szuperhősök: Hogyan formálják a különböző termék- és szolgáltatásmárkák Amerika kapitány és Vasember karakterét a Marvel filmekben?", pp. 591-608, opening at "DOI: 10.35511/978-963-334-499-6-Papp-Vary-Ronky". Every quote in this record was checked to fall inside that chapter; the volume front matter and the other papers carry no vendor mention. Hyphenation inside quotes ("MBTI mo- dell", "Myers-Briggs né- gyest", "16per- sonalities.com") is the retrieved text's own line-break artefact and is reproduced rather than silently repaired.

R1 false: the work administers nothing. It applies the typologies analytically to two fictional film characters and to product brands — Sec. 1 (Bevezetés): "többféle ismert tipológiával próbáltuk meghatározni, hogy a két karakter, Amerika kapitány és Vasember milyen archetípusba tarto- zik." English gloss: we tried to determine with several known typologies which archetype the two characters, Captain America and Iron Man, belong to. No respondent, human or artificial, completed anything. R3 false: no type frequencies or population statistics. R4 false: no reliability or validity figure is sourced to the vendor anywhere; the only psychometric source in the work is Boyle 1995 on the MBTI's limitations, which is not the vendor. R6 false: the character profiles and the Hypothesis 7 and 8 results rest on the vendor's framework, so this is not a passing mention. R7 false: the object of study is product placement in Marvel films; the vendor is a method, not the subject.

C1 false: the work keeps the two apart throughout. The abstract lists four models, "Aaker, Mark&Pearson, MBTI, NERIS Type Explorer"; the section heading is "4.5. Az MBTI modell és a NERIS Type Explorer módszertana"; and the vendor's proprietary fifth axis is attributed to the vendor, not to the MBTI — "Identitás: A hozzáadott ötödik személyiségjegy-páros az eddigieket támasztja alá" (gloss: Identity: the added fifth personality-trait pair underpins the preceding ones), "Az asszertív személyiségek magabiztosak, jól ellenállnak a stressznek." and "A turbulens individuumok tudatosak és igen érzékenyen reagálnak a stresszre." (gloss: Assertive personalities are self-assured and withstand stress well / Turbulent individuals are self-conscious and react very sensitively to stress). What the work asserts is descent, not identity, which is C2.

C3 rests on standing, not uptake: the flag is set on "ezzel egy még pontosabb elemzési lehetőséget biztosítva" (gloss: thereby providing an even more precise possibility of analysis), a comparative accuracy claim for the vendor's test over the published MBTI, and Sec. 6 lists accuracy among its examples and says the adjectives are not a closed list. I did not rely on Sec. 4's "a legnépszerűbb és egyben a primer kutatáshoz legalkalmasabb módszertanokat alkalmaztuk" (gloss: we applied the most popular and at the same time the most suitable methodologies for the primary research), because "legnépszerűbb" is a popularity claim, which Sec. 6 excludes from C3.

Narrow reading (S7): both flags survive it. C2 and C3 rest on sentences that name the vendor's test "NERIS Type Explorer" outright, not on proprietary content attributed to the MBTI without naming the test.

No bundled citation had to be flagged on more than one role. This work is not one of the three Sec. 7 calibration records.

uncertain_note: c1/gate: The work never states that its own authors administered any instrument to anyone; the only 16Personalities mention is a single passing description of the vendor's free test as an alternative to the official MBTI, explicitly noting it 'has [not] been subject to the same validity tests and research of the MBTI specifically' (OVERVIEW OF BEHAVIORAL TRAITS AND CLASSIFICATIONS) — this is a distinction, not a conflation, so C0 is clear and R6 (mention only, no claim rests on it) fits better than R1-R5. The harder call is the E code. The paper is explicitly framed as a synthesis/position piece ('This theoretical paper aims to provide details from existing literature...' — INTRODUCTION; 'Future empirical research is proposed to validate these theoretical findings.' — Abstract), which matches E4's own examples ('reviews, position pieces'). But Tables 2 and 3 report actual quantified MBTI type-frequency percentages (E/I, S/N, T/F, J/P and three-way combinations) for named groups of accounting and non-accounting students, explicitly sourced to 'Andon et al. (2010)' — a separate study, not this paper's own participants — and the Conclusion reasons directly from those percentages to new claims ('those NFPs, NTPs, SFPs, or FTPs, as shown in Table 3... could be better fitted for positions as tax professionals'). That is a literal match for E2 ('Type labels came from an existing dataset... or another study. The authors administered nothing'), not the E1(c) case in §2 (which requires unstated provenance for the work's own named participants — here provenance is stated and the participants are explicitly Andon et al.'s). I coded E2 on the strength of that literal match, but the protocol does not say how to treat a review-genre paper that quantitatively reuses another study's type data as argumentative evidence rather than performing its own secondary analysis of it, so I am flagging the E2/E4 choice as unresolved rather than treating my reading as settled. || c2/gate: E2 vs E4 is the undecided point. Those figures are reproduced from a cited study, Andon et al. (2010). Read literally, E2's 'Type labels came from ... another study' could cover reproduced aggregate frequencies; read as written, E2 concerns type labels the work holds, and this work holds none. I coded E4 because the work reports no type data it obtained, and because §5 fixes the principle that a study's cited literature does not put other people's practice into this work's row — but §5 states that for the R flags only, so extending it to the E code is my inference and not a rule the protocol writes. uncertain_note: c1/gate: This work does not administer any personality instrument to a human respondent or an artificial agent, so E1 and E3 do not apply. The paper's 'subjects' are two fictional Marvel characters (Captain America, Iron Man), characterized via the authors' own qualitative content analysis of 11 films, using several typology frameworks at once (Aaker's brand personality, Mark and Pearson's archetypes, Rogers' innovation adoption curve, Jung/DISC, and MBTI/NERIS). For the MBTI/NERIS piece specifically, the text states 'The NERIS Type Explorer classifies him as a Defender personality type' (Sec. 5.1) and 'The NERIS Type Explorer classifies Stark as a Commander personality' (Sec. 5.2), and each classification traces in the References list to an existing external source (Monica, 2019a and Monica, 2019b — both 16personalities.com 'Avengers personality series' character-profile articles), not to an administration performed by these authors. I coded this E2 ('Type labels came from an existing dataset, scraped profiles, or another study. title: Persönlichkeitstests im beruflichen Kontext
quote_e: "It is based on a critical narrative review of scientific literature, test manuals, and publicly available information provided by test publishers, supplemented by experience gained from their practical use in organizations." — Abstract (English)
uncertain_note: c1/flags: R7 is set on the sentence (identical in the German and English abstracts) 'Der Beitrag untersucht MBTI und 16Personalities, DiSC beziehungsweise Everything DiSC, das Big-Five-Modell, das Enneagramm sowie Gallup CliftonStrengths' / 'This article examines the MBTI and 16Personalities, DiSC and Everything DiSC, the Big Five model, the Enneagram, and Gallup CliftonStrengths', which names 16Personalities as one of six instrument families this critical narrative review examines. Section 5's R7 illustrative examples (a discourse analysis of the vendor's website copy, a survey measuring attitudes toward the vendor's test, an ethnography of a community that took it) are all works whose entire subject is the vendor; here 16Personalities is one of several personality-test systems compared in a broader workplace-testing review, so it is undecided whether R7 was meant to reach a comparative, one-of-several treatment like this one or is restricted to works wholly about the vendor. I chose R7 over R6 because the sentence states the vendor is something the article's own analysis is directed at (not 'named in passing'), and none of R1-R5 fit (no administration, theory-sourcing, norms, figure-bearing psychometric claim, or data-scraping is stated). Also considered and rejected: the pairing 'MBTI und 16Personalities' (echoing 'DiSC beziehungsweise Everything DiSC') lists the vendor's test beside the published instrument with no predicate of identity, provenance, or authority, and with no explicit statement that they are distinct instruments either -- the text is simply silent on the relationship between the two, so C0 stands and states_distinction is not set from list structure alone.
